topic: Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources
subject: chemistry

items.q: A monitoring station in a city records carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulates in the air above a busy road. What do these three pollutants have in common?
items.correct: All three are released when fuels are burned
items.misconception: All three form from nitrogen in the air
items.why: Students learn that the carbon in carbon dioxide and the sulfur in sulfur dioxide both come from inside the fuel, and generalise that pattern to every pollutant. An engine draws in air as well as fuel, and air is about four-fifths nitrogen. At the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Oxides of nitrogen are the one pollutant here whose key element does not come from the fuel.
items.random_wrong: All three come from sulfur in the fuel

items.q: Which statement best describes what most fuels, including coal, contain?
items.correct: Carbon and/or hydrogen, and possibly some sulfur
items.misconception: Carbon and/or hydrogen, and always a little sulfur
items.why: Sulfur dioxide appears in the specification's list of gases released when fuels burn, and students read a list of possible products as a list of guaranteed products. The specification says fuels 'may also contain some sulfur'. Sulfur dioxide is only released if the fuel actually contains sulfur, which is why low-sulfur fuels exist.
items.random_wrong: Carbon and nitrogen, and possibly some sulfur

items.q: A hydrocarbon fuel burns completely in a plentiful supply of air. Which two substances are released?
items.why: Students memorise a list of combustion pollutants without attaching each one to the condition that produces it. With a plentiful supply of air the carbon is oxidised all the way to carbon dioxide. Carbon monoxide appears only when the oxygen supply is limited.

items.q: Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons are released from a burning fuel. What do they form in the atmosphere?
items.why: Particulates are mentioned alongside gases in the same part of the specification about what is released when fuels burn, so students treat them as one more item in a list of gases. The specification separates them: solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates. They are suspended solids, which is why they block sunlight and cause global dimming.

items.q: Petrol is burned inside a car engine and carbon monoxide is found in the exhaust gases. Why is carbon monoxide produced?
items.correct: The oxygen supply is limited, so combustion is incomplete
items.misconception: Nitrogen from the air combines with carbon atoms
items.why: Students learn that the carbon in carbon dioxide and the sulfur in sulfur dioxide both come from inside the fuel, and generalise that pattern to every pollutant. An engine draws in air as well as fuel, and air is about four-fifths nitrogen. At the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Oxides of nitrogen are the one pollutant here whose key element does not come from the fuel.
items.random_wrong: Sulfur in the petrol takes oxygen from the carbon

items.q: Oxides of nitrogen are found in the exhaust gases of a hot car engine. Where does the nitrogen in them come from?
items.correct: From nitrogen in the air drawn into the engine
items.misconception: From nitrogen compounds present inside the fuel
items.why: Students learn that the carbon in carbon dioxide and the sulfur in sulfur dioxide both come from inside the fuel, and generalise that pattern to every pollutant. An engine draws in air as well as fuel, and air is about four-fifths nitrogen. At the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Oxides of nitrogen are the one pollutant here whose key element does not come from the fuel.
items.random_wrong: From sulfur impurities reacting with hot air

items.q: A fuel contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which products are formed?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide, water and sulfur dioxide
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen and sulfur dioxide
items.why: Students think of burning as breaking the fuel apart into its elements rather than as a reaction of the fuel with oxygen. Combustion is a reaction with oxygen. The hydrogen in the fuel combines with oxygen to make water, which appears in the exhaust gases as water vapour.
items.random_wrong: Carbon monoxide, water and sulfur dioxide

items.q: A gas heater burns methane in a room where the air vent has been blocked, so the oxygen supply is poor. Which product now appears that would not be formed with plenty of air?
items.why: Students learn that the carbon in carbon dioxide and the sulfur in sulfur dioxide both come from inside the fuel, and generalise that pattern to every pollutant. An engine draws in air as well as fuel, and air is about four-fifths nitrogen. At the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Oxides of nitrogen are the one pollutant here whose key element does not come from the fuel.

items.q: Carbon monoxide leaks from a faulty boiler into a house. Why is this so dangerous?
items.correct: It is toxic, and colourless and odourless so hard to spot
items.misconception: It has a sharp smell that people learn to ignore
items.why: Everyday experience of smelling exhaust fumes, and of the odour deliberately added to domestic gas, leads students to assume the dangerous gas is one they can smell. The smell of exhaust comes from other substances. Carbon monoxide itself is colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected, which is exactly what makes it so dangerous.
items.random_wrong: It turns the water vapour in the room into acid

items.q: Which pollutants does the specification name as the causes of acid rain?
items.correct: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant students hear about most, so it becomes the default answer for any harmful effect of burning fuels. In this specification carbon dioxide is linked to climate change, not to acid rain. Acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.

items.q: As well as causing acid rain, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen affect people directly. What effect on humans does the specification give?
items.why: Every pollutant gets filed under 'global warming', and the words 'global dimming' and 'global warming' look alike, so students blur the two. Particulates reflect and absorb sunlight on its way in, so less light reaches the surface. That is global dimming. The specification also links particulates to health problems for humans.
items.random_wrong: They make a hole in the ozone layer

items.q: Particulates in the atmosphere cause health problems for humans. What other effect does the specification give for particulates?
items.why: Every pollutant gets filed under 'global warming', and the words 'global dimming' and 'global warming' look alike, so students blur the two. Particulates reflect and absorb sunlight on its way in, so less light reaches the surface. That is global dimming. The specification also links particulates to health problems for humans.

items.q: Under what conditions is soot produced?
items.correct: When the supply of air is limited, so some carbon in the fuel is released as solid particles rather than being oxidised.
items.misconception: Soot is produced when there is plenty of oxygen, because a hotter, fiercer flame burns more of the fuel.
items.why: Students associate soot with a big, hot fire and do not connect the sooty yellow flame with a shortage of air. A plentiful air supply gives a clean flame and carbon dioxide. A limited air supply gives a sooty flame, because carbon is released as solid particles.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is global dimming the same as damage to the ozone layer?
items.correct: No. Global dimming is less sunlight reaching the surface because particulates in the atmosphere block it.
items.misconception: Global dimming means the ozone layer has been destroyed, so light and radiation get through differently.
items.why: Students hold a single 'damaged atmosphere' idea in which ozone holes, dimming and warming are all the same story. The specification links particulates to global dimming and to health problems in humans. Ozone depletion is a separate issue and is not what global dimming means.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.correct: Because it is a toxic gas, and it is colourless and odourless so it is not easily detected.
items.misconception: It is dangerous because it is explosive and will catch fire if there is a spark.
items.why: Students associate any gas leak in a house with a fire or explosion risk, which is the hazard they have been warned about most often. The hazard the specification gives is toxicity. Carbon monoxide poisons people, and because it cannot be seen or smelled they may not realise they are breathing it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does carbon monoxide cause acid rain?
items.correct: No. The specification gives sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen as the causes of acid rain.
items.misconception: Carbon monoxide causes acid rain, because it is a harmful gas released by burning fuels.
items.why: Students group all combustion pollutants together and assume they share all the same harmful effects. Each pollutant has its own effects. Carbon monoxide is toxic; sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems and acid rain; particulates cause global dimming and health problems.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.9.3 Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources
